questions.question: After the code: int x = 10; int *p = &x; *p = 20; what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: p points to x, so assigning *p = 20 directly changes the value of x.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing the element arr[i] of an array?
questions.explanation: Arrays are stored contiguously, so an element's address is computed directly from its index.

questions.question: What is the worst-case complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of a sequential array of n elements (shifting the others)?
questions.explanation: All n elements must be shifted one position to the right.

questions.question: Given int a[5]; int *p = a; the expression *(p + 2) is equivalent to?
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic p + 2 points to element 2 (zero-based); dereferencing it gives a[2].

questions.question: An array allocated with int *a = new int[n]; must be freed how?
questions.explanation: An array allocated with new[] must be freed with delete[]; a plain delete causes undefined behavior.

questions.question: A piece of code has two nested for loops, each running from 1 to n, with a simple assignment as the body. What is its complexity?
questions.explanation: The inner body runs n × n times.

questions.question: What is the complexity of inserting a node at the head of a singly linked list (with a head pointer)?
questions.explanation: Create the new node, set next = head, then update head.

questions.question: What is the worst-case complexity of searching for a value in a singly linked list of n nodes?
questions.explanation: The list is traversed sequentially from the head and may visit all n nodes.

questions.question: To delete the node right after node p (where p->next is not NULL), the correct approach is?

options.text: Save q = p->next; set p->next = q->next; free q
Set p = p->next, then free p
Free p->next first, then set p->next = p->next->next

questions.explanation: The node to delete must be saved, p linked to the node after it, and only then freed; freeing first loses the reference.

questions.question: Compared with arrays, the main drawback of linked lists is?

options.text: Accessing the i-th element takes O(n)

questions.explanation: Linked lists have no random access; they must be traversed from the head.

questions.question: The advantage of a doubly linked list over a singly linked list is?

options.text: It can be traversed in both directions, and a node can be deleted in O(1) when a pointer to it is known
The i-th element is accessed in O(1)

questions.explanation: Each node has an extra prev pointer, so there is no need to traverse again to find the previous node.

questions.question: In a singly circular linked list, where does the next pointer of the last node point?
questions.explanation: The circular property: the last node links back to the first.

questions.question: Which principle does a stack follow?
questions.explanation: The element pushed last is popped first.

questions.question: Which data structure is best suited to check whether a string of brackets ()[]{} is balanced?
questions.explanation: A closing bracket must match the most recent unclosed opening bracket, which is exactly the LIFO property.

questions.question: What is the value of the postfix expression 3 4 + 2 * ?
questions.explanation: 3 4 + gives 7, then 7 2 * gives 14.

questions.question: Performing pop on an empty stack causes which situation?
questions.explanation: Underflow occurs when taking an element from an empty structure.

questions.question: Which principle does a queue follow?
questions.explanation: The element enqueued first is dequeued first.

questions.question: Enqueue 1, 2, 3 into an empty queue, then dequeue once. Which element is at the front now?
questions.explanation: Dequeue removes 1, so the next front element is 2.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a circular queue implemented with an array?

options.text: To reuse the empty slots at the start of the array without shifting elements

questions.explanation: The front/rear indices wrap around, so the free space at the front is not wasted.

questions.question: A recursive factorial function missing its base case (n = 0 or n = 1) will lead to?

options.text: Infinite recursion and a call stack overflow

questions.explanation: With no stopping point, calls keep stacking up until the stack memory overflows.

questions.question: What is the worst-case complexity of Quick Sort?
questions.explanation: When the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, the partition is highly unbalanced.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Merge Sort in all cases?
questions.explanation: The array is halved log n times and merging each level costs O(n).

questions.question: In what order does a preorder traversal of a binary tree visit the nodes?
questions.explanation: Preorder visits the root first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree.

questions.question: With the root at level 0, what is the maximum number of nodes at level i of a binary tree?
questions.explanation: Each level has at most twice as many nodes as the level above it.

questions.question: What sequence of keys does an inorder traversal of a binary search tree produce?
questions.explanation: Left < root < right, so inorder traversal gives a sorted ascending sequence.

questions.question: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 in that order into an empty BST. What is the preorder traversal?
questions.explanation: Root 50, left child 30 (with children 20 and 40), right child 70; preorder: 50, 30, 20, 40, 70.

questions.question: If keys already sorted in ascending order are inserted into an empty BST, what is the search complexity afterwards?
questions.explanation: The tree degenerates into a linked list, so its height is n.

questions.question: What is the balance condition of an AVL tree?

options.text: The left subtree is always taller than the right
All leaf nodes are at the same level
For every node, the heights of its two subtrees differ by at most 1
Both subtrees have the same number of nodes

questions.explanation: The balance factor of every node must be in {-1, 0, 1}.

questions.question: Insert 10, 20, 30 in that order into an empty AVL tree. Which rotation is needed and what is the new root?

options.text: Right rotation at node 30; the root is 10
Left rotation at node 10; the root is 20

questions.explanation: Inserting 30 creates a right-right imbalance at 10, so a left rotation brings 20 up as the root.

questions.question: What is the height of an AVL tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: An AVL tree is always nearly balanced, so its height is proportional to log n.

questions.question: In a max-heap, what is the relationship between a parent node and its children?

options.text: Nodes at the same level are equal
The parent is smaller than its children
The parent's value is greater than or equal to its children's values
The left child is always larger than the right

questions.explanation: As a result, the largest element is at the root.

questions.question: A heap is stored in an array indexed from 0. At which position is the left child of the node with index i?
questions.explanation: With zero-based indexing, the left child is at 2i + 1 and the right child at 2i + 2.

questions.question: Which data structure does breadth-first search (BFS) use?
questions.explanation: BFS visits vertices layer by layer by distance, which matches the FIFO property.

questions.question: Which structure or technique is commonly used for depth-first search (DFS)?
questions.explanation: DFS goes as deep as possible down one branch and then backtracks, which corresponds to a stack or recursion.

questions.question: How much memory does an adjacency matrix of a graph with n vertices take?
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix has n × n entries.

questions.question: A complete undirected graph (every pair of vertices is connected) has 5 vertices. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: The number of edges is C(5,2) = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10.

questions.question: When is an adjacency list usually better than an adjacency matrix?

options.text: When the graph is sparse (few edges)
When the number of vertices is very small
When edge lookup must be O(1) for every pair

questions.explanation: An adjacency list stores only the edges that actually exist, taking O(V + E).

questions.question: What is a collision in a hash table?

options.text: The hash function returns a negative value
Two different keys are hashed to the same position
One key is hashed to two positions
The hash table is completely full

questions.explanation: Because the key space is larger than the number of slots, collisions cannot be avoided entirely.

questions.question: How does collision handling by chaining work?

options.text: Find the next empty slot in the table
Each slot of the table holds a linked list of elements with the same hash index

questions.explanation: Colliding keys are appended to the same list at that slot.

questions.question: With a good hash function and a reasonable load factor, what is the average search complexity in a hash table?
questions.explanation: The key maps directly to the slot to look up, with few collisions.
